.KEY MESSAGES...
Updated at 635 PM EST Wed Nov 18 2026

  - There is an increased threat of urban flooding along the east
    coast of South Florida the next few days. Impactful flash
    flooding is ongoing across portions of SE Florida and this
    risk is expected to continue through tomorrow.

  - Wind Advisory in effect for the eastern metro areas through
    Wednesday night. 
 
  - Flood Watch in effect for all of Southeast Florida through 
    Thursday evening.

  - Dangerous marine conditions continue across local waters with
    sustained winds between 20-30 kts with isolated gusts to 35
    kts. Atlantic seas are expected to climb to 8-12 feet through
    Thursday, with 4-6 feet across Gulf waters.
 
  - Life threatening rip currents and dangerous surf are forecast
    for Miami-Dade, Broward, and Palm Beach beaches through the
    remainder of this week.

&&

.SHORT TERM...
(Rest of today through Thursday)
Issued at 348 PM EST Wed Nov 18 2026

Coastal convergence and pinned thunderstorms along the eastern metro 
area of South Florida continue to bring heavy rainfall and increased 
flooding concerns through the rest of the afternoon. Heavy rainfall 
from last night already led to several flash flood instances along 
metro Miami-Dade and Broward County. Fort Lauderdale is colloquially 
known as "Venice of America" for its vast array of navigable inland 
waterways. Unfortunately, this nickname has taken on a whole new 
meaning with the amount of rain that fell last night. Dual-pol and 
MRMS radar estimates indicate that the areas of Davie, Hollywood, 
Fort Lauderdale, Dania Beach, and Plantation seemed to have gotten 
the largest bull's eye of rain over the past 12 hours. Anywhere 
between 8 to 15 inches of rain have fallen over this area, and it 
has continued to rain so far this afternoon(although much lighter). 
This has lead to several flooded and impassable roadways, along with 
reports of flood waters entering homes and damaging property. Any 
additional rainfall will likely lead to new flash flood warnings and 
rising waters. Remember to never drive, walk or wade over flooded 
roadways. 

The forecast for today and tomorrow still remains quite tricky.There 
is high confidence that widespread rainfall will continue to impact 
the region through Thursday, but the main uncertainty lies with 
where the heaviest rainfall will occur. Aloft, Florida remains under 
the influence of a cut-off low near the panhandle, which will 
continue to provide favorable ascent for storms to maintain 
themselves. SPC mesoanalysis shows an area of more significant upper 
level divergence right off the coast of South Florida, which seems 
to be fueling the heavier activity within Biscayne Bay and over the 
Gulf Stream. However, the features at the surface will best dictate 
where and how much rain will fall. Radar and satellite imagery 
indicate that a few mesoscale low pressure centers are beginning to 
spin within the Gulf, Florida Straits, and over the Atlantic. The 
main rainbands currently pummeling the region seems to be focusing 
along a stationary boundary moving across the keys and into the 
Florida Straits. Current analysis and guidance seems to indicate 
that a deeper area of low pressure is begging to develop off the 
coast of the Florida Keys and moving into the Bahamas. Coastal 
convergence continues to sprout new training thunderstorms, 
particularly along Biscayne Bay and Atlantic coast. With PWATS near 
2 inches, heavy rainfall rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour have been 
observed at several locations. It appears that the current trend 
should have most precipitation continue to focus along Dade county 
over the next several hours, but flooding rainfall is possible 
across all eastern metro areas, with most likely amounts of 2 to 4 
inches and worst case amounts of localized 8 to 10 inches through 
tomorrow. 

The other ongoing concern is strong to gusty winds, particularly 
over Miami-Dade. You may as well change the nickname of Vice City to 
Gusty City considering the fact that several locations across the 
region have had sustained 25 to 30 mph winds and gusts up to 45 mph. 
Much of these strong winds are attributed to a localized 850 mb jet 
of 30 kts across the Gulf Stream. This may be a result of the a 
stronger pressure gradient developing along the coast as surface 
troughing deepens across the Florida strait. Aside from some 
stronger winds aloft mixing down, the pressure difference between 
the rain-cooled air to the east and the warmer and drier environment 
out to the west could be playing a role in speeding things up across 
South Florida as well. A Wind Advisory is in effect for all eastern 
metro areas through 1 am on Thursday, highlighting the potential for 
broken tree limbs and unsecured object being flown around. 

Overnight, winds are expected to weaken down to around 15 kts. 
Rainfall is expected to continue, although it is hard to say how 
heavy it will remain as we head into the early morning hours on 
Thursday. If the developing low pressure center over the Bahamas 
trends more east, we may actually get a lull in activity. If it 
stays closer to the west and near the Florida coast, heavy rainfall 
will be more likely. In any case, there is medium to high confidence 
that coastal convergence storms will continue to pepper the Atlantic 
coast through tomorrow afternoon. However, guidance does seem to 
show a trend in heavier rainfall shifting more north towards Palm 
Beach county through tomorrow night. A Flood Watch does remain in 
effect for Palm Beach, Broward, and Miami-Dade through Thursday. 

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Thursday night through Tuesday)
Issued at 1232 AM EST Wed Nov 18 2026

On Friday, global models depict multiple areas of low pressure 
across the Gulf and western Atlantic. Our original area of low 
pressure remains in the Gulf while an additional lobe of 
vorticity is able to break off into the western Atlantic and 
becomes the dominant feature. Across the eastern CONUS, high 
pressure at the surface begins to breakdown as a cold front sweeps
across the central United States. Before the arrival of drier air for
the weekend, perhaps one additional day of heavy rainfall
potential on Friday, especially earlier in the day as PWATs remain
maximized and will still approach 2". Exact forecast for Friday
will be heavily dependent on the evolution of the surface lows,
however, so I would place confidence on this portion of the
forecast on the lower end for now. The cold front sweeping across
the central CONUS and retreat of high pressure will help pull the
low over the western Atlantic towards the north and finally usher
in drier air across the area through the weekend timeframe. As 
this system deepens and races off to the north, PWATs drop into 
the 1.2-1.3" range and Saturday and continue to fall to perhaps 
below 1" on Sunday and Monday. This should help limit rain chances
through the weekend, although there will still be a chance 
(10-20%) for scattered shower activity each day through the 
weekend and early next week. 

Moisture begins to return heading towards the middle portion of the 
week as an area of low pressure slides across the Gulf states. This 
will likely be our next shot for more significant rainfall although 
details will become clearer over the coming days. 

&&

.AVIATION...
(00Z TAFS)
Issued at 635 PM EST Wed Nov 18 2026

Showers continue across much of eastern South Florida, but some
heavier cells are beginning to develop near KDJT. VFR conditions
should prevail through the period, but some sub-VFR visibilities
and ceilings may be observed near or under showers. Have included
VCTS for the remainder of the evening for KDJT and for tomorrow
afternoon along most eastern locations. Winds will stay quite
breezy, between 15 and 20 kts, with gusts up to 25 kts. 

&&

.MARINE...
Issued at 1232 AM EST Wed Nov 18 2026

Strong northeasterly winds will result in hazardous conditions 
across all local waters of South Florida through the next couple 
of days. Easterly winds between 25-30 kts will be likely through 
the day with isolated gusts to 35 kts possible. 8-12 foot seas are
possible across Atlantic waters over the next couple of days with
4-6 feet across Gulf waters. Small Craft Advisories are in effect
through Thursday night.

&&

.BEACHES...
Issued at 1232 AM EST Wed Nov 18 2026

High risk of rip currents across SE Florida beaches as gusty
onshore flow continues. A High Surf Advisory is in effect for 
Palm Beach County beaches and Broward County beaches as surf 
height could reach 7-10 feet through Thursday.
